summary:
Cross River State falls entirely under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 operates in full within the state: same-sex marriage or civil union, and the registration, operation or participation in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, carry up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide, and the offence reaches anyone who assists, attends or promotes a same-sex relationship or an LGBTQ+ organisation. A visitor who accompanies a partner to a gathering, or who helps organise one, is exposed on the same terms as a resident.

The Criminal Code in force in Cross River separately criminalises sexual activity between men at 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency between men at 3 years.

Cross River is not among the twelve northern states — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara — where religious criminal law applies to same-sex acts and the maximum can be death. Within Cross River the exposure is secular and capped at 14 years; crossing into any of those twelve states materially raises it.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice for Nigeria, reported in August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sexual activity, and of death-penalty risk under religious law in some northern states.

Nigeria offers no anti-discrimination protection to LGBTQ+ people, so there is no official complaint route when a visitor is refused service, threatened or extorted.

Dating apps and social venues carry documented entrapment risk. A nationwide 'kito' scheme lures gay men and trans women to meetings where they are assaulted, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Police profiling produces arbitrary arrest and paid release. The pattern of mass detentions is national: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 held after a hotel raid in Delta in June 2018, 67 arrested in Warri in August 2023 and 76 detained in Gombe in October 2023.

Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion backed by threats and physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. The report is national in scope and describes the machinery a visitor perceived as gay or trans would meet.
tangentialFactors:
The same August 2026 travel advisory that carries the LGBT+ warnings also alerts travellers to short-notice curfews and vehicle-movement restrictions, mobile-network shutdowns announced with little notice, and political rallies and communal violence. None of these are identity-specific, but each narrows the margin for a traveller who needs to move, call for help or reach an exit route at short notice.

The Human Rights Watch research of June and July 2010 covered Lagos, Anambra and Kaduna states and the federal capital as case studies of three of Nigeria's six geopolitical zones. The findings are stated at national level and Cross River is not named in the report, so the police-practice baseline it establishes is applied to Cross River as part of the national pattern rather than on local evidence.

The recorded mass arrests cluster in both halves of the country, in Kaduna and Gombe in the north and in Lagos, Delta and Warri in the south. Cross River appears in none of the reported operations, which indicates that its residents and visitors have not been the subject of large-scale documented roundups rather than that enforcement is absent.
localsOnly:
Residents of Cross River who register, run or take part in an LGBTQ+ organisation commit an offence under the 2014 Act punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the same penalty attaches to publicly showing a same-sex relationship. Organising, hosting or attending is therefore criminal exposure in its own right, independent of any sexual conduct.

The Criminal Code provisions of 14 years for sex between men and 3 years for gross indecency between men apply to residents alongside the 2014 Act, giving prosecutors two statutory routes in the same conduct.

With no anti-discrimination law in force, residents have no statutory claim in employment, housing, healthcare or public service when refused or mistreated on the basis of sexual orientation or gender expression.

Extortion by officers is documented as routine practice rather than isolated misconduct: Human Rights Watch found prolonged unlawful detention used to extract money, with payment the ordinary condition of release, and national monitoring of enforcement conduct recorded 89 extortions, 118 harassment incidents and more than 20 unlawful detentions of LGBTQ+ people by law-enforcement officials in 2024 alone, including detentions for 'looking gay'.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records a prosecution, arrest or police operation under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 or the Criminal Code within Cross River State itself. Local enforcement levels are therefore not established here; the assessment rests on the national framework and national incident data.

Whether proposals to criminalise cross-dressing or public gender expression, reported among transgender Nigerians' concerns, have been enacted into binding law is not settled by the available sources.

The sources do not address gender-marker or identity-document rules, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or the placement of trans detainees between male and female sections in Cross River facilities. Those questions are unsourced here rather than answered in the negative.

The Human Rights Watch material predates the 2014 Act by four years and describes general police corruption; it is used for the institutional pattern of arrest-and-payment, not as evidence of a specific anti-trans operation.
